claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel provides passive protection under room-temperature, non-aggressive salt conditions.
Exposure of Q235 steel to aggressive molten salt at 700–900 °C selectively dissolves or destabilizes its native oxide layer.
Destabilization of the native oxide layer impairs its protective function and accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
The relevant structural mediator is the microstructure and adherence of surface iron oxides such as Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure will cause greater mass loss in Q235 steel than room-temperature moderate-salt exposure.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure will produce spallation or phase transformation of the Q235 surface oxide.
The native oxide on Q235 steel will remain largely intact during room-temperature moderate-salt exposure.
Q235 reference samples held in an inert environment or non-aggressive salt at room temperature will show minimal mass loss and preserved oxide layers.
Alloying or pre-passivation that stabilizes the oxide should prevent the proposed high-temperature degradation mechanism from applying.
The proposed mechanism should not apply when the salt does not interact aggressively with iron oxides.
Short exposures may not permit enough oxide evolution to produce the predicted degradation.
A Cr-Mn-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy exposed to molten FLiBe at 700 °C for 1000 hours lost significant mass relative to 316H stainless steel because Mn dissolved into the salt.
Selective Mn dissolution in the earlier HEA system affected the protective quality of an oxide layer.
